name: Hammurabi
info: Hammurabi was the sixth Amorite king of Babylon, reigning from c. 1792 to c. 1750 BCE, who brought almost all of Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule and issued the law code that bears his name.

facts.born: c. 1810 BCE by convention (the date is unknown); son of Sin-muballit, of the Amorite First Dynasty of Babylon
facts.died: c. 1750 BCE, in the forty-third year of his reign, apparently of illness or perhaps of old age
facts.role: King of Babylon (c. 1792 – c. 1750 BCE); later also king of the lands of Sumer and Akkad, king of the entire Amorite land and king of the four regions of the world
facts.known: the Code of Hammurabi; the conquest of Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari; uniting almost all of Mesopotamia under Babylon; more than 200 surviving letters to his officials; canals, city walls and temple works; edicts of debt remission

t: Hammurabi inherited a kingdom of limited territory with numerous rivals and, in a few years in the second half of his reign, eliminated the major kingdoms of Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari.

His law code, written towards the end of the reign and divided by modern historians into 282 provisions, is the longest legal text to survive from the ancient Near East, though its nature and function are debated.
The empire did not outlast him: his son Samsu-iluna lost the south to revolts, and later ages remembered Hammurabi less as a conqueror than as the ideal lawgiver.
dyk: Hammurabi refused to swear his oath of alliance with Zimri-Lim of Mari on the 25th of the month, apparently a day considered unlucky for invoking the moon god Sin, and took it three days later before his council.
ev: Hammurabi succeeds his father Sin-muballit as king of Babylon and in his first year issues an edict of debt remission
Samsi-Addu dies and his Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia disintegrates; in the struggle that follows Hammurabi allies with Zimri-Lim of Mari
With the help of Zimri-Lim he takes Larsa, brings out its king Rim-Sin alive and annexes the kingdom, gaining the whole lower Mesopotamian plain
He turns on his former ally Zimri-Lim; Mari is captured and then destroyed between 1761 and 1759 BCE
Hammurabi dies in the forty-third year of his reign and is succeeded by his son Samsu-iluna

sections.early:
Hammurabi was born into the Amorite dynasty that had ruled Babylon since around 1880 BCE, when Sumu-la-El made a secondary city without a notable history the centre of a kingdom dominating neighbours such as Borsippa, Kish, Kutha, Dilbat, Marad and Sippar. His father and predecessor was Sin-muballit. The date of Hammurabi's birth is unknown, as is his age at his accession: given a reign of 43 years he may have been very young, though he may also have been in his twenties or even thirties. His family is very poorly known. None of his wives is documented, no brother is named, and one sister, Iltani, became a nadītum, a nun devoted to the god Shamash at Sippar.

Since the fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur in 2004 BCE Mesopotamia had been divided among kingdoms ruled by Amorite dynasties. In the south Larsa, under the long-reigning Rim-Sin, had annexed Isin and Uruk and was Babylon's most threatening rival. To the north-east lay the expansionist kingdom of Eshnunna in the Diyala valley, and in the north Samsi-Addu, a member of the same Amorite clan as the kings of Babylon, had built from Ekallatum on the Tigris what historians call the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia. The meaning of the name Hammurabi, borne by other Amorite kings of the time, is debated; it is most often read as “the ancestor is great”. All dates of the reign are conventional: the most commonly used system, the Middle chronology, places it from 1792 to 1750 BCE, and others would move it by half a century or a century.
sections.rise:
Hammurabi succeeded Sin-muballit in 1792 BCE. In his first year he issued an edict of debt remission, commemorated in the name of his second year as the year in which he “established law and justice in his land”. The first two decades of the reign are poorly documented. The names of its early years refer mainly to public works and offerings to deities. The seventh commemorates the capture of Isin and Uruk, clearly a short-lived raid, since both cities stayed under Larsa; the tenth a victory over Malgium, won with the support of Samsi-Addu and the king of Eshnunna, though that city remained independent.

The death of Samsi-Addu in 1775 BCE was followed by the rapid disintegration of his kingdom and a struggle for northern Mesopotamia between Eshnunna and the new king of Mari, Zimri-Lim, with whom Hammurabi ultimately formed an alliance. From this point the letters found at Mari record events in some detail. The kingdom of Elam, with the support of Babylon and Mari, attacked and subjugated Eshnunna, but did not stop there, and a coalition of Babylon, Mari and other kingdoms formed against it. The Elamites tried to sow discord between Hammurabi and Rim-Sin of Larsa; the two kings uncovered the ruse and allied, though Rim-Sin contributed little or nothing. The Elamites, who threatened the north of the Babylonian kingdom, were repelled with great difficulty, thanks to troops from Mari and other northern kingdoms. The alliance with Mari had been delayed by a dispute over the city of Hit, which was set aside unresolved.
sections.deeds:
Bolstered by the defeat of Elam, Hammurabi launched a lightning war against Rim-Sin with the help of Zimri-Lim, citing Larsa's meagre support and alleged attacks on his territory, and annexed the kingdom in 1763 BCE, gaining the whole lower Mesopotamian plain. A victory over Eshnunna, Shubartum and Gutium is commemorated in the name of his 32nd year. He then made war on Zimri-Lim: Mari was captured and destroyed between 1761 and 1759 BCE, and Malgium suffered a similar fate. Later year names record the defeat of a northern coalition and deportations from the conquered lands; in the process he established his rule over Assur. His titles grew from “king of Babylon” to “king of the four regions” of the world.

The king dug canals, among them one completed in his 33rd year and named “Hammurabi (brings) abundance to the people”, rebuilt the walls of Sippar and restored sanctuaries. Just over 200 of his letters survive, more than for any other Mesopotamian king; about a hundred are addressed to Sin-iddinam, governor of Larsa, on irrigation, troops, taxes, corvée labour and legal cases, and they show the king involving himself directly in provincial affairs and answering petitions from his subjects.

The Code of Hammurabi, written towards the end of the reign and known mainly from a large stele, has a prologue, an epilogue and what modern historians divide into 282 provisions on judicial practice, property, agriculture, finance, family law, assault, the professions and slaves. It is not the oldest Mesopotamian collection of laws, but it is the longest known.
sections.opponents:
Hammurabi's chief adversaries were the kings he had treated with: Rim-Sin of Larsa, an ally against Elam; Silli-Sin of Eshnunna, a commoner enthroned by that city's elites, to whom Hammurabi married a daughter shortly before defeating him; and Zimri-Lim of Mari, whose troops had helped him against Elam and Larsa. The rift with Mari appears to have come from Hammurabi's ambitions in the Jebel Sinjar region. The Mari letters show a skilled negotiator who used his allies while giving them as little as possible, and a ruler whom K. Radner describes as “a volatile and at times rather threatening personality”.

Beyond the image of a just king that he wished to project, his conquests caused widespread devastation, and P. Michalowski points out that he can be viewed as a “tyrant”. He ordered the destruction of the palace at Mari and deported the defeated, as after the Mutiabal revolt. Such acts were not unusual for his time, however, and nothing indicates that he was more brutal than other kings of his era. Some scholars have read his attention to small matters as the mark of a petty ruler, a judgement M. Van De Mieroop calls mistaken. The status of the laws is also disputed: many see them as a scholarly exercise by scribes that describes the law rather than prescribing it, and there is no conclusive proof that judges applied them; others treat them as general solutions drawn from particular cases. According to D. Charpin the empire was probably less the result of a deliberate policy than of the skilful exploitation of successive opportunities.
sections.last:
The end of the Mari archives leaves the last decade of the reign poorly documented. Year names record the defeat of a coalition of northern kings, among them those of Shubartum, Turukkum and Gutium, in the 37th year, and another victory in Shubartum in the 39th. According to D. Charpin, Eshnunna, already greatly weakened, appears to have been destroyed by floods mentioned in the name of the 38th year and by a shift in the course of the Diyala River, and was abandoned. The prologue of the Code, dated to the end of the reign, lists the cities then under Babylonian control, ending with Mari, Tuttul, Eshnunna, Akkad, Assur and Nineveh in the north.

Hammurabi appears to have been physically weakened from his fortieth year. R. Pientka-Hinz has suggested that the works of that year at the sanctuary of Nergal, god of the Underworld, indicate a king already ill and seeking the favour of the god who would soon receive him. A letter of his son Samsu-iluna to the governor of Sippar seems to say that the king was seriously ill and his death imminent, though a break in the tablet prevents the sentence from being fully reconstructed. Samsu-iluna appears to have been ruling at that time, perhaps as regent, and prepared his accession by remitting debts, a measure typically taken by a new monarch. Hammurabi died around 1750 BCE, in the forty-third year of his reign, apparently of illness or perhaps of old age; one text dates the change of reign to the tenth day of the fifth month of the Babylonian year. Samsu-iluna succeeded him.
sections.legacy:
By Hammurabi's death Babylon was the dominant power in Mesopotamia, but the unification was brief. Samsu-iluna lost the former territories of Larsa to revolts and gained nothing lasting in the north, and the dynasty, pressed by the First Sealand dynasty and by Kassite dynasties, was ended by a Hittite attack in 1595 BCE. Hammurabi can nevertheless be considered to have laid the foundations for a unified Lower Mesopotamia, reducing the old royal capitals to provincial towns.

He was declared a god in his own lifetime, and the personal name Hammurabi-ili, “Hammurabi is my god”, became common. Writings from shortly after his death commemorate him for victory, peace and justice; later the lawgiver came to overshadow the conqueror. Scribes went on copying his laws for centuries as writing exercises, the kings of Suhum claimed him as an ancestor more than a thousand years later, and a Neo-Babylonian inscription presents its king as a second Hammurabi.

His name re-emerged in the mid-19th century with the excavation of Mesopotamian sites. Joachim Menant published the first collection of his texts in 1863, and in 1901–1902 a French team unearthed the stele of the Code at Susa, its inscription being translated and published at once by Jean-Vincent Scheil. An early twentieth-century identification with Amraphel of Genesis 14:1 is now largely rejected. He is one of the 23 lawgivers shown in the chamber of the U.S. House of Representatives, and Saddam Hussein placed a bronze statue of him, over 4 metres high, at the entrance to the Iraqi Parliament.

summary: Hammurabi, sixth Amorite king of Babylon (c. 1792 – c. 1750 BCE), turned a kingdom of limited territory into the dominant power of Mesopotamia by conquering Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari. He is best known for his law code, the longest legal text to survive from the ancient Near East. His empire was lost under his son.
references: Marc Van De Mieroop, King Hammurabi of Babylon: A Biography (Blackwell Publishing, 2005)
Dominique Charpin, Hammurabi of Babylon (I.B. Tauris, 2012)
Martha T. Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (Society of Biblical Literature, 1995)
Karen Radner, A Short History of Babylon (Bloomsbury Academic, 2020)
Paul-Alain Beaulieu, A History of Babylon, 2200 BC - AD 75 (Wiley-Blackwell, 2018)
notes: All dates follow the article's conventional Middle chronology (reign 1792-1750 BCE; a revision 1784-1742 is mentioned); the article itself calls them 'clearly inaccurate'.
Birth: the lede gives c. 1810 BC, but the body says the date of birth is unknown; start -1810 with circa true, and facts.born says so.
Conquest of Larsa: the article gives 1763 BC in the narrative and in the debt-remission passage, 1764 BC in the Sources section and '1764/63 BC' in the Larsa section; 1763 used.
Mari: 'destroyed by Hammurabi in 1761 BC' (Sources) and 'captured and then destroyed between 1761 BC and 1759 BC' (Major conquests); event dated c. 1761 BCE with the range in its text.

The article's sentence introducing the war on Larsa says 'launched a lightning war against him' without naming Rim-Sin in that sentence; the context (Rim-Sin's meagre support against Elam) makes it Larsa.
The victory over Eshnunna is dated only by regnal year (name of the 32nd year); no BCE date given, so it is not an event. The Elamite war has no absolute date either.
Accession year 1792 BC, but Sin-muballit's reign is given as 1812-1793 BC in one passage; left out.
The Mutiabal revolt is mentioned once in the article without explanation; kept as the article has it.
The stele's present location (the Louvre) appears only in an external link title, so it is left out. Article writes BC; BCE used here.
